title: Getting Into Azure VMs: Bastion, az ssh, and Run Command
intro: Like AWS, the modern Azure answer to 'how do I log in to a server?' avoids open SSH ports: Azure Bastion, Entra ID-based SSH (az ssh vm), and Run Command for one-off scripts. And when nothing can connect, boot diagnostics show the console.

steps.prompt: Run 'df -h' on vm-web-01 in rg-web-prod without logging in, using Run Command.
expected_commands: az vm run-command invoke --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vm-web-01 --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "df -h"
az vm run-command invoke -g rg-web-prod -n vm-web-01 --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'df -h'
steps.explanation: The root disk is 97% full, found without SSH access.
steps.why: Run Command goes through the Azure VM agent, so it works with no network path to the VM at all. It's the Azure equivalent of AWS SSM send-command. It needs the agent to be healthy, so a VM that's hung or out of disk may not answer.

steps.prompt: Open an SSH session to vm-web-01 in rg-web-prod using your Entra ID identity instead of a key file.
steps.explanation: Logged in as your Entra ID user, using a short-lived certificate.
steps.why: With the AADSSHLoginForLinux extension, access is granted by Azure RBAC roles (Virtual Machine Administrator/User Login) instead of copied keys. Leaving the company revokes access automatically, which key files never do.

steps.prompt: For a VM with no public IP, go through Azure Bastion: connect to the VM with resource id /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-data-prod/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/vm-batch-01 via the bastion bas-hub in rg-network-hub, with Entra ID auth.
expected_commands: az network bastion ssh --name bas-hub --resource-group rg-network-hub --target-resource-id /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-data-prod/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/vm-batch-01 --auth-type AAD
steps.explanation: You're on a private VM through the Bastion host in the hub network.
steps.why: Bastion is a managed jump box: private VMs need no public IP and no inbound SSH from the internet. The resource ID is Azure's universal address for anything: subscription, then resource group, then provider and type, then name.

steps.prompt: vm-web-02 in rg-web-prod won't respond to anything. Read its boot log from boot diagnostics.
expected_commands: az vm boot-diagnostics get-boot-log --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vm-web-02
az vm boot-diagnostics get-boot-log -g rg-web-prod -n vm-web-02
steps.fake_output:
[    4.812] EXT4-fs (sda1): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode
[   92.114] Kernel panic - not syncing: Out of memory and no killable processes...
steps.explanation: The VM ran out of memory at boot and panicked.
steps.why: Boot diagnostics is Azure's version of 'aws ec2 get-console-output': the one window into a VM whose OS won't come up. Enable it on every VM; with managed storage it costs almost nothing.

steps.prompt: List the extensions installed on vm-web-02 in rg-web-prod, to check whether a monitoring agent is the memory hog.
expected_commands: az vm extension list --resource-group rg-web-prod --vm-name vm-web-02 --output table
az vm extension list -g rg-web-prod --vm-name vm-web-02 -o table
steps.fake_output:
Name                        ProvisioningState  Publisher
--------------------------  -----------------  -----------------------------
AzureMonitorLinuxAgent      Succeeded          Microsoft.Azure.Monitor
OmsAgentForLinux            Succeeded          Microsoft.EnterpriseCloud.Monitoring
AADSSHLoginForLinux         Succeeded          Microsoft.Azure.ActiveDirectory
steps.explanation: Both the new Azure Monitor Agent and the retired OMS agent are installed, so two monitoring agents are running side by side.
steps.why: Extensions are software Azure installs into the VM. They're easy to forget and they compete for memory, which matters a lot on small VM sizes. The legacy OMS/Log Analytics agent has been retired in favour of the Azure Monitor Agent; remove the old one after migrating.
